claim: S3 Replication requires versioning enabled on both the source and the destination bucket, and S3 must have permission (an IAM role) to replicate objects on your behalf.
question: What must be true of both buckets before replication can be configured?

values.display: both source and destination buckets must have versioning enabled
Amazon S3 must have permissions to replicate objects from the source bucket to the destination bucket or buckets on your behalf

evidence.quote: Both source and destination buckets must have versioning enabled. For more information about versioning, see Retaining multiple versions of objects with S3 Versioning.
Amazon S3 must have permissions to replicate objects from the source bucket to the destination bucket or buckets on your behalf.

claim: For cross-account replication, the destination bucket owner must grant the source bucket owner permission to replicate with a bucket policy, and the destination buckets cannot be Requester Pays buckets.
question: What extra requirements apply when the source and destination buckets belong to different accounts?

values.display: the owner of the destination buckets must grant the owner of the source bucket permissions to replicate objects with a bucket policy
the destination buckets cannot be configured as Requester Pays buckets

qualifiers.condition: source and destination buckets owned by different AWS accounts

evidence.quote: The owner of the destination buckets must grant the owner of the source bucket permissions to replicate objects with a bucket policy.
The destination buckets cannot be configured as Requester Pays buckets.

claim: With replication configured, trying to disable versioning on the source bucket returns an error until the replication configuration is removed; disabling versioning on the destination makes replication fail with status FAILED.
question: What happens if you suspend versioning on a bucket that has replication configured?

values.display: you must remove the replication configuration before you can disable versioning on the source bucket
if you disable versioning on the destination bucket, replication fails

evidence.quote: If you attempt to disable versioning on the source bucket, Amazon S3 returns an error. You must remove the replication configuration before you can disable versioning on the source bucket.
If you disable versioning on the destination bucket, replication fails. The source object has the replication status `FAILED`.

claim: Replication time depends on object size and can take hours for large objects. Lifecycle rules on the destination bucket use the object's original creation time, not the time the replica arrived.
question: Which creation time does a Lifecycle rule on a destination bucket use for replicas?

values.display: the lifecycle rules honor the original creation time of the object, not when the replica became available
for large objects, it can take several hours

evidence.quote: The time it takes for Amazon S3 to replicate an object depends on the size of the object. For large objects, it can take several hours. Although it might take a while before a replica is available in the destination, it takes the same amount of time to create the replica as it took to create the corresponding object in the source bucket. If a lifecycle configuration is enabled on a destination bucket, the lifecycle rules honor the original creation time of the object, not when the replica became available in the destination bucket.

claim: Cross-Region Replication copies objects to buckets in other Regions and incurs inter-Region data transfer charges that vary by Region pair; Same-Region Replication has no data transfer charges.
question: Does Same-Region Replication cost data transfer, and what does CRR cost extra?

values.display: there are no data transfer charges associated with Same-Region Replication (SRR)
inter-Region data transfer charges vary depending on the Regions that you choose

evidence.quote: Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) is used to copy objects across S3 buckets in different AWS Regions. You might choose the Region for your destination bucket based on either your business needs or cost considerations. For example, inter-Region data transfer charges vary depending on the Regions that you choose.
There are no data transfer charges associated with Same-Region Replication (SRR).

claim: S3 Replication copies objects asynchronously between buckets owned by the same or different accounts. A replication rule replicates new objects written after the rule exists; existing objects, objects that failed earlier and objects that are themselves replicas are copied with S3 Batch Replication.
question: Does a new replication rule copy the objects that are already in the bucket?

values.display: automatic, asynchronous copying of objects across Amazon S3 buckets
replicate new objects written to the bucket
replicate existing bucket contents (S3 Batch Replication)

evidence.quote: Amazon S3 Replication enables automatic, asynchronous copying of objects across Amazon S3 buckets. Buckets that are configured for object replication can be owned by the same AWS account or by different accounts. You can replicate new objects written to the bucket to one or more destination buckets between different AWS Regions (S3 Cross-Region Replication), or within the same AWS Region (S3 Same-Region Replication). You can also replicate existing bucket contents (S3 Batch Replication), including existing objects, objects that previously failed to replicate, and objects replicated from another source.

claim: Delete markers are replicated only when delete marker replication is enabled in the replication rule; then S3 behaves as if the object was deleted in both buckets. Delete marker replication is not supported for tag-based replication rules.
question: Are delete markers replicated, and under what condition?

values.display: if you have delete marker replication enabled in your replication configuration
Amazon S3 will behave as if the object was deleted in both buckets
does not support delete marker replication for object tag based replication rules

qualifiers.condition: delete marker replication enabled in the rule

evidence.quote: Yes, you can replicate delete markers from source to destination if you have delete marker replication enabled in your replication configuration. When you replicate delete markers, Amazon S3 will behave as if the object was deleted in both buckets. You can enable delete marker replication for a new or existing replication rule.
Amazon S3 Replication does not support delete marker replication for object tag based replication rules.

claim: Access points can be used only for operations on objects, such as GetObject and PutObject, not for other bucket operations like deleting buckets or creating replication configurations. When attached to a bucket, the access point policy works together with the bucket policy.
question: What can and cannot be done through an S3 access point?

values.display: you can only use access points to perform operations on objects
the access point policy works in conjunction with the underlying bucket policy

evidence.quote: You can only use access points to perform operations on objects. You can't use access points to perform other Amazon S3 operations, such as deleting buckets or creating S3 Replication configurations.

If your access point is attached to a bucket the access point policy works in conjunction with the underlying bucket policy. You can configure any access point to accept requests only from a virtual private cloud (VPC) to restrict Amazon S3 data access to a private network. You can also configure custom block public access settings for each access point.

claim: An access point has a network origin of Internet or VPC. With network origin VPC, S3 rejects every request that does not come from the named VPC; the network origin is set at creation and cannot be changed afterwards.
question: What does an access point with network origin VPC block, and can the origin be changed later?

values.display: Amazon S3 rejects any request made to the access point that doesn't originate from that VPC
after you create the access point, you can't change its network origin
network origin of Internet

evidence.quote: An access point that's only accessible from a specified VPC has a network origin of `VPC`, and Amazon S3 rejects any request made to the access point that doesn't originate from that VPC.
You can only specify an access point's network origin when you create the access point. After you create the access point, you can't change its network origin.
An access point that's accessible from the internet is said to have a network origin of `Internet`.

claim: To use a VPC-restricted access point, the VPC endpoint policy must grant access to both the access point and the underlying bucket; requests through the access point succeed only then.
question: What must the VPC endpoint policy allow for a VPC access point to work?

values.display: only succeed through an access point if the VPC endpoint policy grants access to both the access point and the underlying bucket

evidence.quote: To use an access point with a VPC, you must modify the access policy for your VPC endpoint. VPC endpoints allow traffic to flow from your VPC to Amazon S3. They have access control policies that control how resources within the VPC are allowed to interact with Amazon S3. Requests from your VPC to Amazon S3 only succeed through an access point if the VPC endpoint policy grants access to both the access point and the underlying bucket.

claim: Bucket policies can still limit a bucket to specified VPCs, but access points give an easier, auditable way to lock all or part of a shared dataset to VPC-only traffic; an Organizations SCP can require that every new access point sets its network origin to vpc.
question: Why use access point network origin controls instead of a VPC condition in the bucket policy?

values.display: an easier, auditable way to lock down all or a subset of data in a shared data set to VPC-only traffic
mandate that any access point created in your organization set the “network origin control” API parameter value to “vpc”

evidence.quote: You can continue to use bucket policies to limit bucket access to specified VPCs. Access points provide an easier, auditable way to lock down all or a subset of data in a shared data set to VPC-only traffic for all applications in your organization using API controls. You can use an AWS Organizations Service Control Policy (SCP) to mandate that any access point created in your organization set the “network origin control” API parameter value to “vpc”.

claim: An access point policy is written like a bucket policy with the access point ARN as the resource. S3 evaluates all relevant policies (user, bucket, access point, VPC endpoint, SCPs and ACLs) when it authorizes a request through an access point.
question: How is a request through an access point authorized?

values.display: you write access point policies like you would a bucket policy, using the access point ARN as the resource
evaluates all the relevant policies, including those on the user, bucket, access point, VPC Endpoint, and service control policies as well as Access Control Lists

evidence.quote: S3 access points have their own IAM access point policy. You write access point policies like you would a bucket policy, using the access point ARN as the resource. Access point policies can grant or restrict access to the S3 data requested through the access point. Amazon S3 evaluates all the relevant policies, including those on the user, bucket, access point, VPC Endpoint, and service control policies as well as Access Control Lists, to decide whether to authorize the request.

claim: IAM and bucket policies are the simplest approach for a small to medium number of datasets but are bounded by the 20 KB bucket policy and 5 KB IAM policy size limits; access points give far more policy space because each access point has its own policy of up to 20 KB and there can be thousands per Region per account.
question: When does one large bucket policy stop scaling, and how do access points help?

values.display: policy size limits of S3 bucket policies (20 KB) and IAM policies (5 KB)
significantly more space for policy statements
thousands of access points per AWS Region per account, with a policy up to 20 KB in size for each access point

evidence.quote: This strategy works, so long as the necessary policies fit within the policy size limits of S3 bucket policies (20 KB) and IAM policies (5 KB), and within the number of IAM principals allowed per account.

An approach that offers significantly more space for policy statements is to use S3 Access Points as additional endpoints for S3 buckets, because each access point can have its own policy. You can define quite granular access control patterns, because you can have thousands of access points per AWS Region per account, with a policy up to 20 KB in size for each access point.

claim: S3 Access Grants maps identities to S3 datasets by prefix, bucket or object, granting read-only, write-only or read-write access to IAM principals and directly to users or groups from a corporate directory through IAM Identity Center.
question: What is S3 Access Grants, and which identities can it grant access to?

values.display: a simplified model for defining access permissions to data in Amazon S3 by prefix, bucket, or object
both IAM principals and directly to users or groups from your corporate directory
read-only, write-only, or read-write access on a per-S3-prefix basis

evidence.quote: S3 Access Grants provides a simplified model for defining access permissions to data in Amazon S3 by prefix, bucket, or object. In addition, you can use S3 Access Grants to grant access to both IAM principals and directly to users or groups from your corporate directory.

With the simplified access scheme in S3 Access Grants, you can grant read-only, write-only, or read-write access on a per-S3-prefix basis to both IAM principals and directly to users or groups from a corporate directory.
S3 Access Grants supports two kinds of identities: enterprise user or group identities from AWS Identity Center, and AWS IAM principals including IAM users and roles.

claim: Lifecycle transitions follow a waterfall: S3 Standard can move to Standard-IA, Intelligent-Tiering, One Zone-IA, Glacier Instant Retrieval, Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Glacier Deep Archive; One Zone-IA only to Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive; Glacier Flexible Retrieval only to Deep Archive.
question: Which storage class transitions does a Lifecycle rule allow?

values.display: a waterfall model for transitioning between storage classes
the S3 Standard storage class to the S3 Standard-IA, S3 Intelligent-Tiering, S3 One Zone-IA, S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, or S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage classes
the S3 One Zone-IA storage class to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage classes
the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class to the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class

evidence.quote: Amazon S3 supports a waterfall model for transitioning between storage classes, as shown in the following diagram.
The S3 Standard storage class to the S3 Standard-IA, S3 Intelligent-Tiering, S3 One Zone-IA, S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, or S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage classes.
The S3 One Zone-IA storage class to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage classes.
The S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class to the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class.

claim: A Lifecycle rule cannot move an object from S3 Glacier Deep Archive to any other class, and from S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval only to Deep Archive. To change an archived object's class otherwise, restore a temporary copy first and then copy the object with the new storage class.
question: Can a Lifecycle rule move an object from a Glacier class back to S3 Standard?

values.display: the transition of objects to the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class can go only one way
can only be transitioned to the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class
use the restore operation to make a temporary copy of the object first

evidence.quote: You cannot use an S3 Lifecycle configuration rule to convert the storage class of an object from S3 Glacier Deep Archive to any other storage class. If you want to change the storage class of an archived object to another storage class, you must use the restore operation to make a temporary copy of the object first.
Objects that are stored in the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class can only be transitioned to the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class.
The transition of objects to the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class can go only one way.

claim: By default a Lifecycle configuration does not transition objects smaller than 128 KB to any storage class, because each transition is a charged request and the savings on small objects can be smaller than the cost; an object size filter in the rule lets smaller objects transition.
question: Why are small objects not moved by Lifecycle rules by default, and how do you change that?

values.display: prevents objects smaller than 128 KB from being transitioned to any storage class
you are charged a transition request for each object
add an object size filter to your Lifecycle transition rules

qualifiers.condition: configurations created before September 2024 keep the previous behavior until modified

evidence.quote: Amazon S3 applies a default behavior to S3 Lifecycle configurations that prevents objects smaller than 128 KB from being transitioned to any storage class. We don't recommend transitioning objects less than 128 KB because you are charged a transition request for each object. This means, for smaller objects, the transition costs can outweigh the storage savings.

To allow smaller objects to transition, you can add an object size filter to your Lifecycle transition rules that specifies a custom minimum size (`ObjectSizeGreaterThan`) or maximum size (`ObjectSizeLessThan`).

note: The September 2024 change of this default is for the changes lens (dated note on the same page).

claim: Moving objects out of a storage class before its minimum storage duration is charged for the rest of that duration, and a single Lifecycle rule cannot chain a second transition before the first class's minimum duration has passed.
question: Can one Lifecycle rule move an object to Glacier Instant Retrieval and then to Deep Archive a few days later?

values.display: you are charged for the remainder of that duration
can't create a single Lifecycle rule that transitions objects from one storage class to another before the minimum storage duration period has passed

evidence.quote: Certain storage classes have a minimum object storage duration. If you transition objects out of these storage classes before the minimum duration, you are charged for the remainder of that duration.
You can't create a single Lifecycle rule that transitions objects from one storage class to another before the minimum storage duration period has passed.

claim: Lifecycle transitions to Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive run asynchronously, so the physical move can lag the rule date, but you are charged at the destination class rate from the date the rule is satisfied. The one exception is a transition to Intelligent-Tiering, where billing changes after the physical transition completes.
question: When does billing at the new storage class start after a Lifecycle transition?

values.display: transitions objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive asynchronously
charged at the destination storage class rate (S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive) starting from the date the lifecycle rule is satisfied
the only exception is transitions to S3 Intelligent-Tiering, where billing changes occur after the physical transition completes

evidence.quote: S3 Lifecycle transitions objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive asynchronously. There might be a delay between the transition date in the S3 Lifecycle configuration rule and the date of the physical transition. You are charged at the destination storage class rate (S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive) starting from the date the lifecycle rule is satisfied, even if the physical transition has not yet occurred.
The only exception is transitions to S3 Intelligent-Tiering, where billing changes occur after the physical transition completes.

claim: A restore makes a temporary copy of an archived object that is available only for the number of days you give in the restore request; afterwards S3 deletes the copy and the object stays archived, and its storage class still reads as Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive. While restored you pay for both the archive and the temporary copy at the S3 Standard rate, and S3 processes one restore request at a time per object.
question: What does a restore from Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive produce, and for how long?

values.display: you must first restore a temporary copy of it
available only for the duration that you specify in the restore request
the object's storage class remains S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive
processes only one restore request at a time per object

evidence.quote: Archived objects are Amazon S3 objects, but before you can access an archived object, you must first restore a temporary copy of it. The restored object copy is available only for the duration that you specify in the restore request. After that, Amazon S3 deletes the temporary copy, and the object remains archived in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
After you receive a temporary copy of the restored object, the object's storage class remains S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
When you restore an archive, you are paying for both the archive (S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive rate) and a copy that you restored temporarily (S3 Standard storage rate).
You can restore an object copy programmatically or by using the Amazon S3 console. Amazon S3 processes only one restore request at a time per object.

claim: Encrypted objects remain encrypted throughout a storage class transition.
question: Does a Lifecycle transition remove encryption from an object?

values.display: encrypted objects remain encrypted throughout the storage class transition process

evidence.quote: Encrypted objects remain encrypted throughout the storage class transition process.
